# Sepsis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Fever and sepsis > Sepsis*

[Original Article Link](/library/xm0E3g)

---

## Summary

Sepsis is an acute life-threatening condition characterized by organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated <u>immune response</u> to infection. Without prompt intervention, patients frequently progress to <u>septic shock</u> and <u>multiple organ failure</u>. The precipitating infection is often bacterial, typically originating in the respiratory, genitourinary, or gastrointestinal systems or in the <u>skin</u> or <u>soft tissue</u>. Clinical features include <u>fever</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, confusion, and signs of the primary infection. <u>Sepsis screening tools</u> (e.g., <u>SIRS criteria</u>, <u>quick SOFA score</u>) incorporating common clinical variables and <u>laboratory values</u> are used to facilitate early identification of sepsis. Favorable patient outcomes rely on early detection, effective resuscitation measures (e.g., aggressive <u>fluid therapy</u> and appropriate use of <u>vasopressors</u>), and early administration of <u>antibiotics</u>. The <u>diagnostic workup of sepsis</u> should occur in parallel with resuscitation efforts and focuses on identifying the site of infection and causative <u>pathogen</u> for definitive treatment.




See also "<u>Sepsis in pregnancy and postpartum</u>" and "<u>Pediatric sepsis</u>."

## Etiology

See also “<u>Etiology of bloodstream infections</u>.”




* Common sources of sepsis: [[1]](/library/PcaWcj)[[9]](/library/_YX579)

* Respiratory: <u>pneumonia</u> (most common cause of sepsis)

* Abdominal infections (e.g., <u>intraabdominal abscess</u>)

* Genitourinary: <u>pyelonephritis</u>

* <u>Skin and soft tissue infections</u>

* Implanted devices (e.g., <u>central venous catheter</u>, <u>port-a-cath</u>, urinary catheter, <u>endotracheal tube</u>)

* Pathogens

* Bacterial: gram-positive bacteria (most common in the US); <u>gram-negative bacteria</u>

* Fungal, viral, or parasitic infection (rare)

* Common <u>risk factors</u>

* Age: < 1 year or > 75 years

* Primary comorbidities (<u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>community acquired pneumonia</u>, <u>bacteremia</u>, <u>alcohol use disorder</u>)

* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (<u>neutropenia</u>, <u>corticosteroid</u> treatment)

* Intensive care or prolonged admission (<u>nosocomial infections</u>)

* Recent <u>antibiotic</u> or <u>corticosteroid</u> treatment

* Invasive medical devices (e.g., <u>endotracheal tubes</u>, intravenous lines, urinary catheters)





> [!TIP]
> Implanted devices are an important <u>risk factor</u> and a common source of infection. [[1]](/library/PcaWcj)




References:[[10]](/library/Ty06ei)[[11]](/library/gy0Fei)[[12]](/library/Sy0yei)[[13]](/library/QcauXj)[[14]](/library/Rxalw5)[[15]](/library/l-avxM)[[16]](/library/N-a-xM)

## Pathophysiology

Sepsis is a hyperinflammatory systemic reaction.



1. * Local activation of inflammatory mediators (<u>complement system</u>, <u>mast cells</u>, <u>macrophages</u>) results in vessel dilation and further release of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> (esp. TNFα, <u>IL-1</u>).
2. * Generalized <u>endothelial</u> disruption → <u>capillary leak</u> → generalized <u>edema</u> due to a shift of <u>intravascular</u> fluid and <u>albumin</u> into the surrounding tissue
3. * <u>Intravascular</u> <u>hypovolemia</u>;   → excessive triggering of the extrinsic <u>coagulation cascade</u> → <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> (<u>DIC</u>) and <u>microvascular</u> <u>thrombosis</u>
4. * Decreased oxygen utilization and tissue <u>ischemia</u>;   → widespread <u>cellular injury</u> → organ dysfunction (commonly multisystem)




> [!NOTE]
> An adequate <u>immune response</u> requires a balance between proinflammatory (antiinfectious) and antiinflammatory signals!




![Effects of endotoxins and exotoxins](media/i2h51jobzgsio8jhpw8umpyt.jpg)

Effects of endotoxins and exotoxins

## Clinical features

* General features

* <u>Fever</u> , chills, and <u>diaphoresis</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Tachypnea</u>

* Generalized <u>edema</u> (<u>capillary leak</u>)

* Features of organ dysfunction (see <u>SOFA score</u>)

* <u>CNS</u> impairment: <u>altered mental status</u>

* Cardiovascular failure: <u>hypotension</u>

* <u>Coagulopathy</u> → <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> → <u>petechiae</u>, <u>purpura</u>

* <u>Liver</u> failure: <u>jaundice</u>

* <u>Kidney failure</u>: <u>oliguria</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u>; : symptoms of <u>acute respiratory distress syndrome</u> (<u>ARDS</u>)

* Features of <u>septic shock</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u> (<u>MAP</u> < 65 mm Hg)

* Altered <u>skin</u> and <u>soft tissue</u> <u>perfusion</u> 

* Early presentation: warm <u>skin</u> and normal <u>capillary refill time</u> (warm <u>shock</u>)

* Late presentation: cold, <u>cyanotic</u>, pale, and/or mottled <u>skin</u> and prolonged capillary refill time (cold <u>shock</u>)

* Features of the primary infection: e.g., <u>clinical features of pneumonia</u>, <u>meningismus</u>, <u>peritonitis</u>, <u>clinical features of pyelonephritis</u>, <u>clinical features of infective endocarditis</u>

## Management

The following recommendations are consistent with the 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines and the American College of Emergency Physicians (<u>ACEP</u>) task force consensus statement for adults with suspected sepsis in the emergency department. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)




> [!WARNING]
> Sepsis is a <u>medical emergency</u>. Be vigilant for early <u>signs of sepsis</u> and begin treatment as soon as sepsis is suspected.




### Approach [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




Perform diagnostics and treatment simultaneously in patients with suspected sepsis.




* Sepsis surveillance

* Use a <u>sepsis screening tool</u> to identify at-risk patients following local protocols.

* Consider empiric management of high-risk patients even if screening tools are negative. [[18]](/library/lCcvHe0)

* Initial evaluation

* Perform a clinical evaluation using the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* Establish <u>IV access</u>, <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>, and continuous <u>pulse oximetry</u>.

* Obtain the following initial studies immediately:

* Serum <u>lactate</u>: Elevated <u>lactate</u> predicts sepsis severity and helps guide resuscitation.   [[19]](/library/UMbbL8)[[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* Two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) prior to <u>antibiotics</u> (if possible)   [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[21]](/library/xJ0EwS)

* See “<u>Septic workup</u>” for additional investigations that are typically included in initial studies.

* Initial management: Provide <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u> and <u>respiratory support</u> for unstable patients without delay.

* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u>: Infuse 30 mL/kg of <u>crystalloid</u> fluid in 3 hours.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[22]](/library/APbRhF)

* <u>Vasopressors for septic shock</u>; : Administer if <u>hypotension</u> persists (during or after <u>fluid resuscitation</u>); target <u>MAP</u> ≥ 65 mm Hg. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* <u>Antibiotics for sepsis</u>: Begin empiric broad-spectrum or directed <u>antibiotics</u> within 1–3 hours.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[22]](/library/APbRhF)[[23]](/library/skbt6F)

* Next steps

* Continuous reassessment of <u>hemodynamic parameters</u>

* <u>Supportive care for sepsis</u>.

* Begin <u>source control for sepsis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Sepsis management</u> is an iterative process requiring frequent reassessments. Favorable outcomes depend on early detection, effective resuscitation, and early administration of <u>antibiotics</u>. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)




![Sepsis 101: Diagnosis and Treatment](media/small_6108217f8a225.jpg)

Sepsis 101: Diagnosis and Treatment




### Hour-1 bundle for sepsis [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[22]](/library/APbRhF)




* Definition: a group of critical measures that should be performed within 60 minutes of recognizing patients with <u>septic shock</u> or a high <u>pretest probability</u> (<u>PTP</u>) of sepsis. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[22]](/library/APbRhF)[[23]](/library/skbt6F)

* Five essential elements

* Obtain serum <u>lactate</u>.

* Draw <u>blood cultures</u> prior to <u>antibiotic</u> administration.

* Begin rapid IV fluid bolus if <u>MAP</u> < 65 mm Hg or <u>lactate</u> â¥ 4 mmol/L.

* Use <u>vasopressors</u> to keep <u>MAP</u> ≥ 65 mm Hg.

* Administer <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u>.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Hour-1 bundle</u>: <u>lactate</u> + cultures + fluids + <u>vasopressors</u> + <u>antibiotics</u>




### Disposition [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




* Admit unstable patients with sepsis to the <u>ICU</u> within 6 hours.

* If available, consider using a <u>critical care transition program</u> for patients discharged from <u>ICU</u> to other hospital settings after stabilization.

* Consider transfer to a <u>rehabilitation</u> program upon <u>hospital discharge</u> for patients with the following:

* <u>Mechanical ventilation</u> for > 48 hours

* <u>ICU</u> stay > 72 hours

## Diagnostics

The main goals of the diagnostic workup in a patient with suspected sepsis are to determine the presence and severity of organ dysfunction and to identify the source of infection. See the “Definitions” section for diagnostic criteria. [[1]](/library/PcaWcj)[[4]](/library/35YSPp)[[22]](/library/APbRhF)




> [!TIP]
> Positive cultures are not mandatory for the <u>diagnosis of sepsis</u>.




### Sepsis screening tools [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)




* Goal: early identification of patients with sepsis to reduce mortality  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[24]](/library/6CcjGe0)

* Commonly used tools  [[24]](/library/6CcjGe0)

* <u>SIRS criteria</u>  [[1]](/library/PcaWcj)[[3]](/library/3xaSw5)

* Quick SOFA score (<u>qSOFA</u>)  [[25]](/library/DLc1-10)

* Can predict poor outcomes; not recommended as a sole screening tool for sepsis  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[26]](/library/tLcXz10)[[27]](/library/FLcgz10)

* Considered positive if ≥ 2 of the following are present:

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mm Hg

* <u>Respiratory rate</u> ≥ 22/min

* Limitations: <u>Accuracy</u> is low and can vary.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[27]](/library/FLcgz10)[[28]](/library/8LcOz10)





> [!WARNING]
> The <u>qSOFA score</u> is not recommended as a sole screening tool for sepsis or <u>septic shock</u>. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




![qSOFA Score in Septic Patients](media/f6y6v48ak10axllfkssdytx0.jpg)

qSOFA Score in Septic Patients




### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




In addition to serum <u>lactate</u> and <u>blood cultures</u> (at least two sets), obtain the following studies to support the diagnosis and evaluate for organ dysfunction.




* <u>CBC</u>: variable findings

* <u>Leukocytosis</u> or <u>leukopenia</u>

* <u>Thrombocytosis</u> or <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>CRP</u>, <u>procalcitonin</u>: typically elevated  [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* <u>BMP</u> and <u>electrolytes</u>

* Renal function: ↑ <u>BUN</u> and ↑ <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Glucose</u>: <u>hyperglycemia</u>, <u>hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> derangements

* <u>Liver chemistry</u> and synthetic function tests: <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u>, ↑ <u>INR</u>, ↑ <u>ALT</u>, ↑ <u>AST</u>

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>, <u>D dimer</u>: ↑ <u>prothrombin time</u>, ↑ <u>activated partial thromboplastin time</u>, ↓ <u>antithrombin III</u>, ↑ <u>D dimer</u> may be present (see “<u>Disseminated intravascular coagulation</u>”)

* Consider <u>amylase</u>, <u>lipase</u> (if <u>pancreatitis</u> is suspected)

* <u>Blood gas</u>: to identify possible <u>acid-base disturbances</u> and assess oxygenation





### Identifying the source of infection




#### Microbiology




* In addition to <u>blood cultures</u>, consider additional cultures guided by clinical judgment (see “Etiology”).

* <u>Urinalysis</u> and <u>urine culture</u> (See “<u>Urinary tract infection</u>” and “<u>Pyelonephritis</u>”)

* <u>Sputum</u> culture (See “<u>Diagnosis of pneumonia</u>”)

* Consider also: <u>CSF</u> , wound secretion, tissue/fluid

* Diagnostic procedures as indicated to obtain samples for cultures (e.g., <u>lumbar puncture</u>, <u>thoracentesis</u>, <u>paracentesis</u>, <u>arthrocentesis</u>)

* <u>Pan cultures</u> are discouraged unless the source of infection is unclear.  [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)





> [!WARNING]
> When possible, obtain the additional samples before starting <u>antibiotic</u> treatment, but do not delay <u>antibiotics</u> if samples are not rapidly available.




#### Imaging




Direct decisions based on clinical suspicion. Examples of commonly performed imaging include:




* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: if <u>pneumonia</u> is suspected and/or to determine if <u>ARDS</u> is present as a complication (see “<u>Diagnosis of pneumonia</u>”)

* <u>Abdominal x-ray</u>: if a perforation or obstruction is suspected (<u>pneumoperitoneum</u>, <u>air-fluid levels</u>)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>

* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: initial abdomen assessment in most cases (see “<u>Diagnosis of acute abdominal pain</u>”)

* <u>Soft tissue</u>: initial assessment of <u>cellulitis</u> and, in most cases, <u>soft tissue</u> <u>abscess</u> (see “<u>Skin and soft tissue infections</u>”)

* <u>CT scan</u>: for a more detailed assessment of thoracic and abdominal/<u>pelvic</u> pathology

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: to identify valve vegetations (see “<u>Infective endocarditis</u>”)

## Resuscitation and reassessment

See also “<u>Immediate hemodynamic support</u>” and “<u>Septic shock</u>.”




### <u>IV fluids</u>[[29]](/library/-ZcDVa0)[[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




* Initial <u>fluid resuscitation</u>: rapid infusion of 30 mL/kg <u>crystalloid</u> fluid   [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)

* Indication: sepsis-induced <u>hypoperfusion</u> or <u>septic shock</u>

* Timing: Initiate immediately and complete within 3 hours.

* Ongoing IV fluid management  [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* Continuously reevaluate <u>fluid responsiveness</u>.

* See “<u>Hemodynamic reassessment in sepsis</u>.”

* Consider <u>albumin</u> if a large volume of <u>crystalloid</u> fluid has been given.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)





### Vasopressors for septic shock [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[23]](/library/skbt6F)




See “<u>Septic shock</u>” and “<u>Vasopressors</u>” for further details.




* Indication: persistent <u>hypotension</u> during or after <u>fluid resuscitation</u>

* Target: <u>MAP</u> ≥ 65 mm Hg [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* First line: <u>norepinephrine</u> DOSAGE   [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* Second line: Consider adding <u>vasopressin</u> DOSAGE if <u>hypotension</u> persists with moderate doses of <u>norepinephrine</u>.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* Third line: Consider adding <u>epinephrine</u> DOSAGE  if <u>hypotension</u> persists despite <u>norepinephrine</u> AND <u>vasopressin</u>. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* Refractory tissue <u>hypoperfusion</u> : Consider adding <u>dobutamine</u> DOSAGE OR switching to <u>epinephrine</u> alone. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)





> [!TIP]
> Consider starting <u>vasopressor</u> infusion through a <u>peripheral IV</u> to avoid delays while awaiting <u>central venous access</u>. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




### Hemodynamic reassessment in sepsis [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)[[23]](/library/skbt6F)[[30]](/library/k4bmjF)




Continuously monitor <u>hemodynamic parameters</u> and <u>volume status</u> to guide <u>IV fluids</u> and/or <u>vasopressor</u> therapy.




* <u>Hemodynamic parameters</u>  [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[31]](/library/kmbmf8)

* <u>Vital signs</u>: <u>mean arterial pressure</u>, <u>heart rate</u>, <u>respiratory rate</u>

* Clinical indicators of organ <u>perfusion</u>: <u>capillary refill time</u>, urine output, mental status

* Biomarkers: serum <u>lactate</u> , <u>base excess</u>

* Advanced monitoring: <u>cardiac index</u> and <u>stroke volume</u>, <u>echocardiography</u>

* <u>Fluid responsiveness</u> assessment  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* <u>Passive leg raise test</u>

* <u>Fluid challenge</u>

* Consider adding <u>IVC ultrasound</u>.  [[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)[[32]](/library/CGXqY-)[[33]](/library/ZhXZcB)[[34]](/library/ahXQcB)

* Consider protocolized resuscitation targets.

* <u>Lactate-guided fluid resuscitation strategy</u>

* <u>Early goal-directed therapy</u>

* Protocols targeting <u>capillary refill time</u> ≤ 3 seconds [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[30]](/library/k4bmjF)[[35]](/library/9CcN8e0)





> [!TIP]
> If possible, use <u>invasive BP monitoring</u> to facilitate continuous reassessment. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




### <u>Respiratory support</u> [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[36]](/library/yCcdue0)[[37]](/library/_Cc5ue0)




Respiratory dysfunction is a common feature of sepsis. Patients with sepsis frequently have <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>signs of increased work of breathing</u>, and/or <u>hypoxia</u>.




* Start <u>oxygen therapy</u> as needed.  [[38]](/library/rLcf_10)

* <u>Secure the airway</u> and assess for <u>indications for invasive mechanical ventilation</u>.

* See “<u>High-risk indications for mechanical ventilation</u>.”

* See “<u>Hemodynamic compromise in mechanically ventilated patients</u>.”

* Consider screening for <u>ARDS</u> to ensure early identification.  [[37]](/library/_Cc5ue0)

* See “<u>Global definition of ARDS</u>.”

* See “<u>Lung-protective ventilation strategy</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Shock</u> and <u>metabolic acidosis</u> are both associated with a high risk of peri-<u>intubation</u> mortality. [[4]](/library/35YSPp)[[39]](/library/FBYgc7)




### <u>Corticosteroids</u> [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[17]](/library/YPcnWc0)




* Administer <u>stress dose corticosteroids</u> to patients with <u>risk factors for adrenal crisis</u>.

* Consider adjuvant IV <u>corticosteroids</u> if there is an ongoing need for <u>vasopressor</u> therapy.  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* Typical agent: <u>hydrocortisone</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

---

## Infection control

### Approach




* Begin <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u> as soon as possible after sepsis is identified, ideally after <u>blood cultures</u> have been drawn. [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* <u>Shock</u> or probable sepsis : Administer <u>antibiotics</u> within 1 hour.

* Possible sepsis and no <u>shock</u>: Initiate rapid investigation; administer <u>antibiotics</u> within 3 hours if concern for sepsis persists.

* Low <u>probability</u> of sepsis and no <u>shock</u>: Do not start <u>antibiotics</u>; continue patient observation.

* Follow local <u>antimicrobial stewardship</u> guidelines.

* Choose empiric therapy based on:

* Source of infection

* Local <u>prevalence</u> of common and resistant pathogens

* Prior infections, immune status , and comorbidities

* Presence of implanted devices (e.g., urinary catheter, <u>central lines</u>)

* Narrow therapy once the <u>pathogen</u> and <u>antibiotic sensitivities</u> have been identified. [[4]](/library/35YSPp)

* Ensure <u>source control for sepsis</u> as early as possible.





### Empiric antibiotic therapy for sepsis [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[40]](/library/gmbFU8)[[41]](/library/SmbyU8)[[42]](/library/A3bROt)[[43]](/library/kIYm1q)




There is little consensus regarding the optimal <u>empiric antibiotic</u> regimens for patients with sepsis and <u>septic shock</u>, especially if the source of infection is unclear.




#### Evident source of infection [[4]](/library/35YSPp)




If the source of infection is clear, follow local hospital protocols to administer <u>antibiotics</u> that cover the most common causative pathogens.




| Common sources of infective pathogens and their treatment |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | <br>Common pathogens <br> | Treatment |
| Respiratory tract | <br><u>Streptococcus pneumoniae</u>, <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>,  [[44]](/library/y8Yd6I)<br> | See “<u>Treatment of pneumonia</u>.” |
| <u>Urinary tract</u> | <br><u>Escherichia coli</u>, <u>Proteus</u> spp., <u>Klebsiella</u> spp., <u>Pseudomonas</u> spp. [[45]](/library/u9Yp6r)[[46]](/library/4f13mT0)<br> | See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for complicated pyelonephritis</u>” and “<u>Antibiotic</u> treatment of <u>complicated lower UTIs</u>.” |
| Intraabdominal | <br><u>E. coli</u>, other <u>Enterobacteriaceae</u> (e.g., <u>K. pneumoniae</u>), <u>Pseudomonas</u> spp., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>anaerobes</u> (e.g., <u>Bacteroides spp.</u>) [[47]](/library/bpYHLJ)<br> | See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for intraabdominal infections</u>.” |
| Bone or <u>soft tissue</u> | <br><u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp. (including <u>MRSA</u>), <u>P. aeruginosa</u>, <u>Enterobacteriaceae</u>, <u>anaerobes</u> [[48]](/library/kObmsF)[[49]](/library/xzcEEU0)<br> | See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for skin and soft tissue infections</u>” and “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis</u>.” |
| Cardiovascular | <br><u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Enterococcus</u> spp., <u>HACEK organisms</u> [[50]](/library/0pXeL_)<br> | See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for infective endocarditis</u>.” |
| Reproductive tract | <br><u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Chlamydia trachomatis</u>, <u>Neisseria gonorrhoeae</u>, <u>E. coli</u>, <u>Listeria monocytogenes</u>, <u>anaerobes</u> (infection is often polymicrobial) [[51]](/library/QAdujs0)[[52]](/library/fEakEm)<br> | See "<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for pelvic inflammatory disease</u>" and "<u>Empiric antibiotics for maternal sepsis</u>.." |
| <u>Hospital-acquired infections</u> (<u>HAIs</u>) | See “Overview of the most common causative pathogens in <u>HAIs</u>” and “<u>Multidrug-resistant organisms</u>.” | See “<u>Overview of HAI management</u>.” |





#### Unclear source of infection [[40]](/library/gmbFU8)[[41]](/library/SmbyU8)[[42]](/library/A3bROt)[[53]](/library/7Nb4c8)




The following regimens are examples commonly mentioned in the literature; follow local hospital protocols when available.




| <u>Empiric antibiotic</u> regimens for sepsis with unclear source |  |

### <u>Antifungal</u> therapy [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)




* <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>fungemia</u> include:

* <u>Immunocompromised</u> status (e.g., <u>neutropenia</u>, transplant, <u>chemotherapy</u>)

* Indwelling vascular devices (e.g., <u>hemodialysis catheters</u> or <u>central lines</u>, <u>TPN</u>)

* Prolonged <u>antibiotic</u> courses

* Consider empiric <u>antifungals</u> (in consultation with an ID specialist) for high-risk patients only, e.g., those with: [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* Severe sepsis or <u>septic shock</u>

* Recent treatment with other <u>antifungals</u>

* Suspected resistant <u>Candida</u> species

* Treatment options: see “<u>Treatment of invasive candidiasis</u>” for dosages.

* <u>Echinocandins</u>: e.g., <u>micafungin</u>, <u>caspofungin</u>, <u>anidulafungin</u>

* <u>Azoles</u>: e.g., <u>fluconazole</u>, <u>voriconazol</u>

* Liposomal formulations (if the patient can not tolerate <u>echinocandins</u>): e.g., <u>amphotericin B</u>





### Source control for sepsis [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)[[23]](/library/skbt6F)




Identify and eliminate sources of infection that cannot be adequately treated with antimicrobials as soon as possible (e.g., within 6–12 hours).  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)




* <u>Remove infected intravascular catheters</u> or devices after replacement with an alternative.

* Arrange drainage of contained infections (e.g., <u>abscesses</u>, <u>cholangitis</u>) and/or surgical resection of infected tissue

* Consult the appropriate specialty for definitive treatment of the infectious source, e.g.:

* <u>Surgery</u> for:

* <u>Acute abdomen</u> (e.g., <u>peritonitis</u> due to <u>GI perforation</u> or <u>ischemic</u> bowel)

* Most <u>abscesses</u>

* <u>Necrotic</u> tissue (e.g., <u>necrotizing fasciitis</u>)

* Infected implanted devices

* Interventional radiology for:

* <u>Nephrostomy</u> or drain placement in obstructive <u>pyelonephritis</u>

* Percutaneous drainage of intrathoracic or <u>intraperitoneal</u> <u>abscess</u>

## Supportive therapy

* Fluids, nutrition, and <u>electrolytes</u> [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[42]](/library/A3bROt)

* <u>Maintenance fluids</u>: Consider after initial <u>fluid therapy</u> for stable patients at risk of <u>hypovolemia</u>.

* Aim for <u>euvolemia</u>.

* See “<u>Clinical signs of fluid balance</u>” for details.

* Bowel rest or enteral feeds: indication depends on the source of infection and <u>level of consciousness</u>

* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u>

* <u>Transfusions</u>: Consider as needed. [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[42]](/library/A3bROt)

* <u>pRBCs</u> for the following <u>hemoglobin</u> thresholds:

* < 7 g/dL in all patients

* < 10 g/dL in patients with cardiac <u>ischemia</u>, severe <u>hypoxemia</u>, or severe bleeding

* <u>Platelets</u> for the following <u>platelet count</u> thresholds:

* < 10,000/mmÂ³ in all patients

* < 20,000/mmÂ³ in patients with a high risk of bleeding

* < 50,000/mmÂ³ in patients with active bleeding or planned <u>surgery</u> or invasive procedure

* <u>FFP</u> to <u>correct coagulopathy</u> in patients with active bleeding or a planned invasive procedure

* Other supportive measures [[20]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[42]](/library/A3bROt)

* <u>Normoglycemia</u>: <u>insulin</u> as needed for target <u>glucose</u> of 140–180 mg/dL (see “<u>Inpatient management of hyperglycemia</u>”)

* <u>VTE prophylaxis</u> with <u>LMWH</u> if there are no contraindications [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* <u>Stress ulcer prophylaxis</u> in patients with <u>risk factors</u> for <u>GI bleeding</u>  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)

* <u>Renal replacement therapy</u> (<u>RRT</u>) in patients with absolute <u>indications for RRT</u>  [[2]](/library/ILcY_10)
